speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The necessity for this amendment arises from the fact that at the last session of the legislature of Ontario the official titles of the superior courts of that province were altered. They were formerly the appellate division of the Supreme Court of Ontario and the high court division of the Supreme Court of Ontario. These names have been altered, and the former names of the Court of Appeal of the province of Ontario and the High Court of Justice for Ontario have been established. In 1913 section 32 was inserted in the Interpretation Act to comply with the then titles of these courts. Now there is nothing necessary but to repeal that section and allow the old section to stand, because the old names have been re-established.

Section agreed to.
On section 2.-Date of commencement.
I did not hear the first part of my hon. friend's remarks. Is there a change in the names of the courts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it is proposed to repeal section 32 of the Interpretation Act, which was inserted in 1913 when the names were changed to the appellate division of the Supreme Court of Ontario and the high court of justice of the Supreme Court of Ontario. These names were adopted in 1913, and section 32 was placed in the statute to meex that change. At the last session of the legislature the old names of the Court of Appeal of Ontario and the High Court of Justice of Ontario were re-established, so if we strike out section 32 it allows the Interpretation Act to apply in respect of the former and the present names.

Then we get back practically to where we were in 1913? That is, the old court of appeal was changed in 1913 to the appellate division, and now we have the first and second appellate divisions. These names are being changed back to the Court of Appeal and the High Court of Justice, the high court of justice including the circuit courts. I believe there is some change, is there not, with regard to the chief justices of the different courts?

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 108, to amend the Companies Act.
He said: This bill incorporates two proposed amendments to the Companies Act. The first section is an amendment to subsection 2 of section 33 which, in its present form, provides that the company shall in no case make any loan to any shareholder of the company.
Some years ago a number of the large industrial companies in Canada and some of the larger mining companies, particularly the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, made arrangements whereby their employees might subscribe and pay, usually by instalments, for shares of the company by which they were employed, on a basis satisfactory to the company and to them, so as to identify the employees more completely with the company. Subsequently, during the past year or so, housing schemes for employees have been proposed and are being carried out by a number of these companies, the proposal being that the company should advance money to employees who desired such advances or loans, to enable such employees to build or acquire their own homes. These schemes have become very popular indeed, particularly since the fall in the price of building material and the abundance of labour have enabled such schemes to be carried out on a very large scale at a minimum of cost.
The objection has been raised that those of the employees who, in years past, have invested some of their savings in five, ten, fifteen or twenty shares of the company by which they were employed, thereby became shareholders of the company, and it has been contended that by the existing section the company is precluded from making any loans or advances to such employees in connection with these building and housing schemes. I have gone very thoroughly into this question, and this amendment is one upon which I have set my heart. I thought the present law precluding such assistance being given to employees was not wise and should be amended. Therefore I have introduced this amendment in section 1 of this bill. I commend it to the favourable attention of the

house; I have spent some time studying the question and I think it is a perfectly proper amendment and one that should be approved by the house.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.
On section 1-Loans.

Is it the idea of the minister to avoid the common practice of companies erecting the dwellings themselves, leasing them and absolutely controlling them by that process? In other words, will there be more freedom for thie employees?

It has been represented to me that the employees prefer this scheme to the system of leasing. They prefer to own their homes in fee simple, and this is a departure from the old practice to that extent.

Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: INCREASE IN MEMBERSHIP OF PENSION TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
The Pension Act was
amended at the last regular session. Its provisions were not operative until about seven or eight months ago, and so, as amended, it has been in operation for so brief a period ihat the time has not been sufficient to demonstrate its perfections and imperfections. It is not proposed, therefore, to deal in any sense with the provisions of the act generally; but it has become very obvious that the various boards that consider pensions are not able to deal with the large number of applications that are being made. The amended Pension Act of last year was widened in its scope, and this resulted in a largely increased number of applications. For instance, those applicants who previously had accepted a small amount of commuted pension have now been made eligible for reinstatement. This has resulted in something like 18,000 men being added to the list of those who may or may not be eligible for reinstatement. The provisions of the act are also broader in respect of the benefit of the doubt as well as in affording every pensioner an opportunity to come forward, even if his case had been refused by the federal appeal court. Altogether, the number of applicants for pensions cannot be dealt with by the tribunal at present in existence for that purpose. It was thought wise to facilitate as far as possible the operation of the act in the way of expediting hearings. These amendments do nothing more than take such steps in a moderate way as may assist in expediting the hearing of eases. I do not expect that the increased number of members of the board suggested in the amendment will be sufficient to avoid all delay, but in any case it is an effort to reduce the period of waiting of a substantial number of men. It will mean that probably several
thousand cases will be taken up each year which otherwise would not be dealt with under the present procedure. It is proposed to add three members to the pension tribunal, which will permit of two sections acting at the same time. There are other details of the amendment which I think could be discussed when the bill goes to the second reading. Another change is in the procedure so far as the pension board is concerned. Instead of the tribunal acting in the way it does under the present act, it is proposed that much of the work will be transferred to the pension board as a first board to permit of action being taken there instead of being submitted to a subsequent board. The pension board has been in existence for something like ten years, while the pension tribunal has been in existence for only eight months. I believe the work can be carried on more readily by a well trained board than by a new organization. It may be of interest to the house to know that these amendments have proved satisfactory to the headquarters of the legion.

speechtext:
No debate can take place
at this time. It may be that I was moving a little fast when I put the first reading, but the minister's statement can be treated as an explanation on the first reading, and the motion is not open to debate.
Scientific institutions - expenses connected with the Dominion observatory at Ottawa, $66,880; expenses connected with the Dominion astrophysical observatory at Victoria, B.C., $25,170.

Mr. Chairman, I inquired of the minister the reason for the dismissal or retirement from the observatory branch of the Department of the Interior, of five employees and on June 22 he informed me that they had been retired so that returned soldiers might be taken into the service. I would like to know why these five permanent employees were retired so that returned soldiers might be taken into the service. I have no objection to returned soldiers being employed, but I would like to know why it was necessary to retire five permanent employees.
Hon. THOMAS G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior): Mr. Chairman, the Department of the Interior is considered as a unit and when the staff was being reduced in the department it was not divided into water-

Supply-Interior-Observatories
tight compartments. Certain regulations or rules for guidance were laid down and those rules were followed out in all departments.

There may be some
reason for these retirements, but I cannot get it. Apparently there were five people on the outside looking into the service and five permanent employees are retired. There may be a valid reason but up to the moment I have not been able to get it. If the minister will give me an answer which I can understand I am quite willing to allow the item to go through, but until that answer is given I am afraid I will have to oppose this item.
I do not know that I can give any further answer to that already given.

It was highly improper that $850,000 should be appropriated for salaries without an investigation as to whether or not that would be sufficient to carry on the service. The observatory does not fall within those branches affected by the transfer of the natural resources. If these men were over the age of sixty-five years and were entitled to superannuation, there might be some reason for their being retired. I have received a letter from the wife of a man who was employed in the observatory, from which I desire to quote certain portions. This letter is dated June 28, and reads:
The whole time my husband worked there everything seemed satisfactory and he has the very best of references from Mr. R. Meldrum Stewart and Mr. J. P. Henderson. It was quite a surprise that he was let out being a returned man with four years service in the army, married, and with two children. It was also very hard on the family as up to date we have not got one cent from the government and as you know we have our rent, gas and light and the usual expenses of living which we cannot meet, as Mr. Pilon has been unable to obtain work elsewhere. Those people do not seem to care who are responsible for the holding up of retirement money. It will not be very much, about $26 a month, $336 yearly as Mr. Pilon was only in the service for eleven years. Up to three weeks ago we managed to get our living but since then we have been getting help from the Red Cross.
What is the sense of such action? There may be some valid reasons why these five men were let out, but in the face of this letter and in the face of the so-called explanation of the minister, I must insist on knowing the reason why Mr. Pilon, if the minister wants the man's name, was retired as one of these five men. I want to know why this man who has a wife and two children living was retired andi replaced Iby another returned man. This may be a joke or something else, but surely the minister has some reason to

give for retiring these five men and replacing them by others.

I think I have made the matter quite clear to the committee.
* Mr. CHEVRIER: Not to me.

I say I think I have made the matter quite clear to the committee. The transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces certainly reduced the services which the various branches of the Department of the Interior formerly performed. Owing to the transfer of the resources and the consequent reduction in services, numerous employees would be affected. Their positions would be abolished because there was no further work for them to do. When these reductions were being made during the present fiscal year, certain rules were framed on which the departmental heads acted with the knowledge and cooperation of representatives of the Civil Service Commission. In canvassing the situation we might find that certain employees in this branch or that, taking into consideration the department as a whole, would be affected. Certainly they would, whether they were in the geodetic, topographical or some other branch of the service which might not be directly affected by the transfer. But we are taking the department as a whole, not considering any branch as a water-tight compartment with the employees not being directly affected by the transfer, and such employees, being part of the department, enter into the scheme the same as the others. In the carrying out of these rules which were framed for the guidance of departmental heads, these employees were affected just as if they were in another branch which was directly affected by the transfer. I do not think I could make the matter any plainer than that.
The minister, in connection with the reduction in staff, made a survey of all the branches of the department?
Yes.
No branch was immune? Retirements took place from nearly every portion of the Department of the Interior?
Practically so.
So that in these retirements it would appear there were five from the observatory.

Yes.

Supply-Interior-Observatories
And those five were replaced from some other branch, the personnel being thus maintained at the same number?
Yes.

I am willing to go a considerable distance with the minister; I know he had a very difficult situation to handle which has resulted in a tremendously difficult outcome, not only in this city but throughout Canada and particularly in the western provinces. I am going to repeat: The cat is now coming out of the bag. The reason why large numbers of retirements were made was not because these branches were affected by the transfer of the natural resources, but because the Prime Minister, in order to balance or to endeavour to balance the budget, saw fit to say that instead of granting $1,500,000, fie would grant only $850,000 to the Department of the Interior, and therefore the minister would have to cut his coat according to the cloth. As a result of that, rightly or wrongly, justly or unjustly, the knife had to be applied somewhere. In the Dominion observatory there was no reason why any reduction should have occurred because the minister himself has said so. As reported on page 1300 of Hansard, when I asked the minister what branches were affected by the transfer of the natural resources, the minister replied that the dbservatory was not affected by such transfer. Nevertheless, they proceed to lop off five of those observatory employees. I have no great quarrel with the fact that they have replaced those employees by five others who were let out from somewhere else, but there was no justification in the first place, under the guise of the transfer of the natural resources, for retiring those five employees and then substituting five others from another branch of the department. I cannot make the situation any plainer; the minister cannot make it any plainer, and I must leave it at his own door to say that the whole thing has been done through lack of proper representation being made. These men have been let out; they have been replaced by other people who have come from within the service. I have no quarrel to find with that but the saving effected is only $4,670. I suppose the minister would say that this great saving is due to the transfer of the natural resources. What I am going to ask the minister is this: "What positions were vacated by these five employees who were let out in the classification of positions in the observatory? Were these positions abolished? Were they of a temporary nature? If they are of a permanent nature, why retire these five employees and substitute others? Is this just a scheme to let these people out and then at a later date endeavour to fill up all these positions with other people?

If the hon. member will look at page 86 of the estimates, which we are not dealing with at the present time, he will find at the bottom of the page the explanation of the sum which he mentioned, namely, $850,000. It reads:
The sum of $850,000 is submitted pending the final adjustment of staffs by the department and the Civil Service Commission, owing to the transfer of natural resources, such sum to cover allowances to those who may be retired and salaries of those retained.
Necessarily in making the reduction, the exact amount could not be known or estimated until the situation was fully canvassed and the services which were to be continued were decided on. Then and then only could one know the exact amount which would be required. In the meantime this sum was put in tentatively until that readjustment and reorganization could take place. In this reorganization the department was considered as a unit, and not as a system of watertight compartments. I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that I could make it any plainer to the committee than I have already done.

I take it that the reason why these five employees were let out was not because of the transfer of the natural resources but purely and simply because the minister found himself with an appropriation of $850,000, whereas in the past he had an appropriation of $1,500,000. I would like to ask why one of these employees, a returned soldier by the name of Pilon, was retired to be replaced by another returned soldier.

The employees who were notified of their retirement certainly were affected by the transfer of the natural resources in the manner I have indicated. I cannot allow the hon. gentleman to get away with that statement. Certainly they were affected by the transfer of the natural resources because they were in the Interior department and the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces undoubtedly did affect that department to a very great extent. In the readjustment all employees had to take their chance-shall I say?-of retirement, whether they worked in a branch of the department that was directly affected by that transfer or not. Some branches were, of course, more directly affected in that sense than others, but they should have their rights
Supply-Interior-Surveys

in the service considered in just the same manner as those working in a branch which was not so directly affected by the transfer.

I take it
that that was the policy of the government in making the adjustments, that all branches were to be surveyed? Take, for example, the lands branch, which was transferred practically in its entirety. The Northwest Territories branch, however, was not affected by the transfer, but, nevertheless, as it was a branch of the department, and as it was the policy of the government that all branches should be surveyed in the readjustment, retirements took place, I presume, in that branch and in all other branches.
I think that every branch of the department was affected.

Was that
the policy of the government in dealing with this matter? That, notwithstanding the fact that this particular branch was not affected in personnel, yet as it was a branch of the Interior department, a survey had to be made of it along with all the other branches, and retirements took place in practically every branch?
Practically.

That may be all right,
but I am not prepared to accept that in view of the letters I have.

I merely
want to say to the hon. member that we now have declared the policy of the government on which these retirements took place. It seems to me, however, that it is quite proper to ask why retirements took place in any branch that was not directly affected by the transfer.

Quite so, and I have
the minister's answer, which I quoted a moment ago, that this branch was not affected by the transfer.
I said it was affected.

Oh no, as I will show
to the minister. Here is the letter that retired Mr. Pilon. First there is the memorandum:
The services of Mr. L. R. Pilon have unavoidably had to be dispensed with through the operation of the present departmental reorganization.
Then here is the letter retiring Mr. Pilon, dated April 29, 1931:
Dear Mr. Pilon,-	,
It is regretted that the reduction in the amount available for the continuing work of this department makes it necessary to terminate your services from and after to-day.
[Mr. Murphy.)
So his retirement was not due to the transfer of the natural resources, and the minister is in a hopeless situation when he tries to maintain that. He might as well be frank about it and say that in a number of instances retirements were due to that cause, but that in a number of other instances, and particularly in this case, the retirements were not due to that cause. In the case of these employees of the Dominion observatory who were retired, the retirements were certainly not because of the transfer of the natural resources, because here is the letter of the department itself stating that "the reduction in the amount available for the continuing work of this department makes it necessary to terminate your services from and after to-day." If the minister will cease to sail under false colours and will say that these employees were retired, not because of the transfer, but because they had not been taken care of by the previous administration, we will agree, but I cannot let the minister get away with his present explanation.

Item agreed to.
Topographical Surveys
Topographical and aerial surveys and maps for the general development and administration of the country, including hydroelectric, forested, mineralized, agricultural and industrial areas; expenses of Geographic Board of Canada; centralization of all aerial photographic operations in cooperation with the Royal Canadian Air Force; traverse of northern rivers and lakes for administration of Northwest Territories; legal surveys of Dominion lands; surveys for administration of Dominion parks; testing of standard measures and instrument repairs; plotting and printing of maps and plans, etc., $250,000.
Amount required to pay the fees of the board of examiners for D.B.S. of the secretary and of the subexaminers and for travelling expenses, stationery, printing, rent of room and furniture, etc. (the fees of Messrs. F. H. Peters, W. M. Tobey and Harry Parry, members of the board, and J. A. Cote, secretary, are to be paid out of this sum), $2,000.
What services are going to be discontinued in connection with the topographical surveys?

Speaking generally, there
will be a reduction in the survey work which the department has been carrying on. The subdivision surveys formerly carried on by this department will not be carried on at all except in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, and very little will be done there. The topographical survey and photographic work is still being continued, with the aerial work being done, as formerly, by the National Defence department.

Supply-I nterior-Surve ys

I presume
that because of the reduction of $180,000 in this vote a number of topographical surveyors will be retired. That would account for part of this reduction. As to the balance, is there to be any topographical survey work in the way of aerial surveys done in the three prairie provinces this year, or are they on the same basis as the other provinces of Canada?

The Department of
National Defence, through the Royal Canadian Air Force, is carrying on in the western provinces on about the same scale as in previous years.

There is
no reduction in that work?
Practically none.

How many
topographical surveyors are there on the staff now? What reduction has been made in the numbers of that staff?
The total number of permanent retirements was eighty-seven.

How many
remain?

One hundred and
eighteen.

At page 1300 of Hansard of May 6, the hon. minister, in answer to a question of mine, said that in the surveys bureau there has been ninety-one retirements of the permanent staff at Ottawa, and that subsequently six more had been retired. At this date how many have received notices of retirement from the topographical survey?

On May 6 nine were
retired.

In the answer to which I have referred of May 6, the minister stated that in the surveys bureau ninety-one of the permanent staff at Ottawa had been retired and twenty-five of the non-permanent. That, does not make very much difference, but I should like to know how many of the permanent staff in Ottawa of the topographical surveys have been retired to this date.
To date eighty-seven have been retired.
What is the personnel of the permanent staff?
On June 20 the remaining staff numbered one hundred and eleven

I believe the topographical survey is one of the most important
branches of our surveys, and it has been my privilege on a number of occasions to meet the men engaged in that work. Probably some members derive pleasure from reading novels, but I derive pleasure from reading maps, and I must pay a particular compliment to the various map services of the federal government. To my mind the topographical survey is one of the services that should never have been interfered with.
Carried.

My hon. friend will not get a bit further by trying to help the minister in that way. Anyone who has not an intelligent suggestion to make should keep quiet. I do not believe that this appropriation is sufficient to carry on the work of the topographical surveys in an efficient manner during the present fiscal year. It seems to me that any saving that may be made in this branch and in the geodetic and geologic branches will be more than offset by the extra cost which will be involved in resuming the work at the point where it has been left off, to say nothing of the mental anguish and suffering of those who have been so ruthlessly let out. I do believe that the minister would have been well advised in the national interest to have retained the staff at its full strength and so have preserved the efficiency of the service. Will the eighty-se\ en positions vacated in the topographical service be left vacant or will they be abolished?

The eighty-seven retirements related to positions which were formerly filled, some by surveyors and others by those doing clerical work. It is not correct to say that eighty-seven surveyors were let out of that branch; eighty-seven employees were let out. The hon. member expresses concern that owing to these retirements the branch will not be efficiently carried on, but just a moment before he had expressed confidence in the officials. I may say that I have the same confidence in them, and I can assure the hon. member that the work in that branch will continue to be efficiently performed. It may be that in certain lines they will not be as active as they were in other years, but I feel confident that the efficiency of the branch will be maintained during the present fiscal year.

The minister will recall that on a former occasion I asked him what branches were affected by the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces, and what number of employees were affected.
Supply-Interior-Surveys

According to his answer of the 6th of May to which I have already referred, the survey bureau was one of the branches not affected by that transfer. Why were the eighty-seven retired? And when will the activities of this branch be resumed?

The work of the surveys
bureau, sometimes known as the international boundaries surveys branch of the department, as such of course was not affected by the transfer of the resources, 'but again this branch was considered part of the Department of the Interior and some clerical positions were affected. They had to take their chances along with the rest of the employees of the department.

The minister told the hon. member for Ottawa that there were 111 employees retained on this staff, but he told me there were 118 retained. I can quite understand how that difference might have arisen, but the question I wanted to ask was .this:	Has the survey and readjustment of the department as far as the staff is concerned been completed? Has it been decided finally in what way the staff shall be re-adjusted, or is that survey still going on?

No, it could not be said
that it has been completed; that is the case to a great extent, but there is still some reorganization and reclassification of positions which will be carried on by the Civil Service Commission.

But as far
as the number of employees is concerned there is not likely to be very much of a change?

That might be taken
practically as correct, although I would not say so definitely.
Does that answer apply to the whole department or only to this branch?

I was speaking of the
department as such.

In connection with the return of the natural resources to the western provinces a case has been brought to my attention disclosing a condition which does not seem fair or reasonable. It is the case of a man who for the last thirty-five years had been working under the Department of the Interior in western Canada. When the natural resources were handed over to the provinces this man was retired. He will receive his full salary for the next six months, and

after that, for the rest of his natural life he will receive approximately seven-tenths of his salary. In the meantime, however, this man has been taken over by the province; he is working at the very same job and getting the very same pay.

I think the government have made another blunder, amongst many they have made since taking power, in transferring this work to the Department of Agriculture. I am certain that they have made a blunder in this particular case because I happen to have had the administration of the branch doing this particular work. It is a branch of the department

that has rendered splendid service to western Canada. No one will deny that. There may be something to be said for the change on the ground of inspection, but the men who actually inspected the land and laid out the program for the preparation of the soil and the planting of the trees were all men trained in the forestry branch and under the control of the Department of the Interior. The work having been such a success, a change of this character is a retrograde step, and I protest against it as strongly as possible. I have nothing to say against the present Minister of Agriculture. I would have protested just as vigorously had my friend and colleague the Minister of Agriculture in our own government attempted to take this important service into his own department from the Department of the Interior. I cannot help thinking there was some attempt on the part of the government to transfer these stations to the provincial governments. If there is any such thing in the mind of the government I for one am going to protest vigorously and keep on protesting, because this service is too important to be interfered with in any way. It oovers the three prairie provinces, and probably eventually will extend into the other provinces. I think it is a work that can be well done by the federal government. If this federal government is going to carry on scientific investigation in tree-planting and technical research in timber and such like matters, then why in the name of conscience take away as important a service as this is to the western people from the branch which has made such a splendid success of it? I view this change with a good deal of apprehension. We had a most enthusiastic band of men in charge of this work, particularly the man at Indian Head, who inaugurated the work and changed the face of a barren country there to a splendid forest in a very short period of time. I cannot help but think that the government is making a very serious blunder in making this change, and I say 22110-213
this without casting any reflection at all on the Department of Agriculture. It is true that I am a farmer and I know something about agriculture, but I do not pretend to know all its intricacies. I do, however, want to protest most vigorously against this change, particularly if an attempt is going to be made by this government to turn the operation and maintenance of these stations over to the provinces.

I feel some sympathy for the Minister of the Interior. I think he was the victim of a general desire to cut expenses. As each minister would bring his estimates before the treasury board or the cabinet there would be a general ripping into them all around, with all the enthusiasm of new converts desirous of doing something. This particular item is one of the victims. I understand that no provision was made at all for this work originally in the estimates, and that the question of transferring the work to the Department of Agriculture, regardless of its merits or demerits, was entirely a second thought. 1 am very glad, however, that the service is going to be continued by some department. There never was a time in the history of our country,-not only this spring and summer, but also last winter-when we needed shelter on the prairies more than we do now, and for the federal Department of the Interior to think of eliminating this work at this particular time seems ridiculous, although I realize it is only on a par with a hundred other things which this government has done since it came into power. I am glad that in this particular instance the mistake was corrected before it was too late, and perhaps it will be in order for me to extend congratulations that the work is going to be continued. It was an awful thing for the government even to contemplate doing away with this service. I do not believe it was the Minister of the Interior who thought of it. I think that as a western man he would have been delighted to have the work continued in the way it was being done. Ministers have to be crucified from one angle or the other, but in this instance the crucifixion did not continue quite to the end, and the service has been salvaged up to a certain point. We must make the best of it, I suppose, and we shall no doubt get the trees through some department. I do not feel so strongly as the former Minister of the Interior over what department has charge of this work, but certainly I should not like to see it handed over to the provincial authorities. It has been administered well from Ottawa,

Supply-Interior-Forestry

and it affects not only one province but the three prairie provinces. One of the things that at the present time is adversely affecting agriculture in the west is lack of shelter against the ghastly hurricane winds that we have been having during the last few years, and anything that will mitigate that evil should be welcomed, no matter from what department it comes. I repeat, I would not like to see the work turned over to the provincial authorities, but the particular department of the federal government by which it is administered is not a matter of so much concern to the people out on the prairies.

I was happy to concur
in the opinions expressed by the former Minister of the Interior, and I am very happy to concur in the expression of view as given by the ex-Minister of Agriculture. When I said that this was a national obligation I used that term in a broad sense, and I do not think I need to retract it. Forestry is one of the four basic industries of Canada, and as such I believe it is incumbent upon the federal government to keep at least a supervising eye upon the preservation of our forests and the work of reforestation. True, responsibility for the protection of the forests may devolve in some degree upon the provinces, but if the decrease in this item will result in any way in prejudicing the safeguarding of our forests, I must strongly protest against it. If I understand the situation, and if I am wrong I want to be corrected, the transfer of the natural resources included the turning over to the western provinces of the care of a certain amount of forest territory in the west.
All of it.

I do not know just what binding agreement was made between the federal and provincial governments, or whether the western provinces incurred the responsibility of keeping up the work of forestry protection to the same degree of efficiency which has been maintained by the federal department up to this moment. But if we have divested ourselves of that responsibility, then it is too late to speak about it. If there are any other portions of Canada where we have not so divested ourselves, then I do ask that the minister be careful that the decrease represented by this item does not in any way interfere with the efficiency of the protection. If the minister will assure the committee that where the protection is continued it will be maintained at 100 per cent, I shall be satisfied.
Carried.

I wish to endorse what my
hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) has said with regard to the services rendered by the tree nurseries at Indian Head and Sutherland. I am at a loss to
know whether the work has been abandoned, is being abandoned, or is about to be abandoned. I personally set out 3,600 trees. Before being given the trees the inspector was sent around to see that the land was in proper shape; his o.k. was necessary before I received the trees. After they are planted he comes around year after year-he was there last fall-to inspect them. That gentleman now is laid off; he will come around no longer, and I am wondering how that work is to be continued. Some time ago, I think, I read that some nine inspectors had been laid off. If the inspectors are laid off there will be no land inspection and no supervision of the trees that have been planted. Is that not evidence on the face of it that the work is to be discontinued? If that is so I wish to protest against it most vigorously. If there is one thing we need in that prairie country it is trees and more trees, and the government that should be responsible for putting in those trees is the federal government. As another hon. member has said, the provincial governments have .[DOT]a little more than they can handle now, and if in the interests of economy the federal *government have laid off some men in the tree planting division, I sincerely hope they will give further consideration to this service and carry it on as efficiently as it has been carried on in the past, and in fact I will go so far as to say that it should be carried on a little more efficiently in the future. The hon.
member for Kindersley has raised the question of the dismissal of inspectors. I think the minister should inform the committee how many inspectors have been dismissed, and for 1 what reason.

The work which has been carried on at the Indian Head and Sutherland stations is being continued in its entirety. By that I mean to say that the work which

has been done at the stations themselves is being continued in full. The orders for trees sent in a year ago have been filled, and the work at the stations is still going on as it did in former years.
There were a number of inspectors whose services were of an outside nature, such as various hon. members have described, among the farmers themselves. They inspected the ground, gave advice as to its preparation and later inspected the care given these trees by the settler. Those nine inspectors have been retired, but the Department of Agriculture assured me that their officials, the men connected with the various experimental farms or plots throughout the west will continue the work formerly done by those men. I may say also that one of the provincial governments has been very anxious to cooperate with the Dominion government in extending that work. As it was outlined to me, their proposition is that they will utilize their gaoi farms and asylum farms so that this work will be greatly augmented in the future, which will meet the wishes of the hon. member for Kinderseley. Whether in these times which have come upon us the ardour of the province will be dampened I do not know, but I can say that the province of Saskatchewan was very enthusiastic in the matter. In that province the problem of soil drifting is perhaps more acute and this service is possibly more appreciated than in the other provinces where we have more of the natural woods. However, I think I can assure the hon. gentleman definitely that the work which has been carried on in the stations themselves is being continued, at least at present, with no curtailment whatever.

I quite appreciate the necessity for very largely reducing the staff of the Department of the Interior, but I believe the forestry branch needs a full staff, particularly of technical men. I understand that certain very well thought of technical men in the forestry branch have been let out, and I should like to ask the minister how many technical men have been let out from that branch, and the reason for that action being taken.
I am informed that before the transfer there were 48 foresters, technical officers, and I am told that the present number is 23.

Can the minister give me the reason why these men were let out, and in what order they were dismissed. Who were dismissed first, who were dimissed next, and so on?

Supply-Interior-Forestry
Those first retired from the service would be such men as fire rangers. They are not technical men.
I mean the technical men.

And men who carried on studies in those areas in western Canada. When the Dominion government administered the forests there, a greater duty devolved upon it to serve those areas than rests upon it at the present time, for the reason that the areas in question were under the crown in the right of the Dominion and the Dominion government actually administered them. There would be more men retired in the west at the time of the transfer than in other parts of Canada where we were not charged with the same administrative duties as in the three prairie provinces. I cannot give the order in which they were retired, but it has been going on now for a period of seven or eight months, and possibly longer.

I was particularly interested in the forestry engineers. Surely there must have been some system under which the men were let out. I presume that those who were over a certain age would be let out first, while those with large families, or with families at all, would be given consideration before those who had no dependents. I take it that returned men would have a preference. Has not the minister some regulation to go by?

The first ones to be notified of their retirement would be those whose positions were abolished. After the readjustment throughout the department the same rules applied to these men as applied to other employees in the various branches of the department.
I take it for granted that returned men, if competent, would have a preference and be given an opportunity to stay on 'before those who had never seen war service.
I can only give the general rules that were laid down.
That is what I want.

Preference is given in the following order, provided always that no employee will be retained unless efficient to perform the service. That is to say, efficiency is the first test. Then there are these rules or regulations: (1) Those who enlisted in Canada and saw active sendee in any theatre of war and have now domestic responsibilities. (2) Other employees with domestic responsibilities. (3) Those who enlisted in Canada
and saw active service in any theatre of war and have no dependents. (4) Others with any dependents. Generally speaking, it will not be possible to retain any employee who has reached the age of sixty-five years and who has put in the full thirty-five years of service, unless such retention is a matter of special necessity to the department.

I have in mind a forestry engineer, a returned man who spent several years on the other side. He is very well qualified and is married. He was let out after a few hours' notice. No consideration has been given him and no reasons assigned for his dismissal. Nothing has been said with regard to his work, which I believe has been most satisfactory throughout his time of service. Why men of that calibre, doing efficient work in the department-men who have seen overseas service-should be let out on such short notice is a matter that calls for explanation.

I presume that
some of these retirements were due to the fact that there was really no vote to pay them all. This service, valuable as it is, is going through a period of orphanage-the department has charge of it. I presume they are paying the staff out of some contingency vote until they get their real vote in the supplementary estimate^. That, I take it, is the condition of affairs; otherwise they would not be paid at all, which, of course, is unthinkable. So that I can imagine the department retiring some of the staff until they get a proper vote to pay them. After that they will take up the work with the same vigour and force that has hitherto characterized it. Am I right in these assumptions?
I have already said that the work is being carried on with the same vigour as before at the stations themselves.

It is hardly fair to men who have been in the civil service for years, men who chose that calling because there was in it the promise of permanency, to find th'emselves on an occasion of this kind, owing to the transfer of a particular branch to another service, thrown out-seven or eight of them-and officers, also permanent, with whom I have no fault to find, given work to do in another department. I understand that the inspection work is now to be done by the inspectional staff of the Department of Agriculture. I am not suggesting that the department should be loaded up with excessive inspectional work. But at the same time there is something to be said for the permanent

Supply-Interior-Water Power
official who, when a transfer is made, loses his job while a permanent civil servant in another branch takes it up. In that case the position cannot be said to have been abolished. I protest against a situation of that kind and I hope that the minister will extend to unfortunate individuals who have lost jobs in this way every assistance in order to place them in some other branch of the service.

Item agreed to.
For investigations of water and power resources and of international waterway problems, the Dominion hydrometric survey, the western provinces water board, and for the administration of the Dominion Water Power and Irrigation Acts, etc., $250,000.

I appreciate the fact that there is a considerable reduction in the service in this particular branch. Is this all owing to the fact that this service will not be required in the three prairie provinces? They will take over many of the services we formerly performed-. Can the minister give us the reduction of staff in that branch?
In August, 1930, the total number of employees at Ottawa and outside Ottawa, 164; in May of the present year, at Ottawa and outside Ottawa, 92.

I notice
there is a total decrease in this vote of $2,764,053. Is that all due to the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces?

It is, to a great extent.
However, there are reductions in other sections of the vote, such as the parks vote, which would not be affected by the transfer.

Are there
other reductions due to the transfer of the natural resources?

There is a reduction of
$30,000 in the item to provide for the construction of the Golden-Revelstoke highway. There is a reduction of $124,660, in the vote for scientific investigations. These reductions are caused by the transfer and I will explain them when we reach the particular items.

Do I understand the
minister to say that the reduction of $277,082 in the parks item is due to the transfer of the resources?

I said it was not.
{Mr. C. A. Stewart.]

To what extent does
the transfer of the natural resources affect the $225,000 reduction in the item covering investigations of water and power resources?

Prior to the transfer the
Dominion government administered the various water powers lying within the different provinces.
That has all been transferred?
Yes. Except those within the national parks.

In 1930 the vote was
$475,000, and it has been reduced to $250,000 for this year. If that branch has been discontinued why should this amount be asked for? I know that a considerable part of this branch still remains in the department. If all the water powers were turned over to the provinces no vote would be necessary.

While the provinces now
administer their own water powers, there are certain services which the Dominion still performs. We have agreements with some of the provinces whereby we are obligated to carry out certain hydrometric measurements of streams. We have one agreement with the maritime provinces, another with Ontario and others with the western provinces. The government also carries on a study of the various waiter problems which affect this country and our neighbours to the south. There are many intricate and pressing problems upon which expert advice is needed at all times, and this branch carries on these studies and advises the government accordingly.

I happen to know the
value of this branch of the department; other branches are important, but so is this one. According to a return made on May 6, there are twelve permanent and three temporary employees in Ottawa and twelve permanent and three temporary employees out of Ottawa who have been notified of their retirement. Is this reduction the result of a proper investigation, and if so, by whom was it made?

The reduction is brought
about by the smaller amount of service to be rendered by this branch.

The minister could say
in a few words the number of employees whose work related to the western provinces. It would seem as though an arbitrary reduction of $225,000 was arrived at. Was there an investigation and did someone go through the department to weed out the employees and say who was to stay and who was to go?

Supply-Interior-National Parks

The head of the branch
*working with the knowledge of and in cooperation with the Civil Service Commission determined who should remain. He determined the stall which in his opinion was best qualified to carry on the services of that branch of the department.

On May 11, the minister answered a question which I asked by saying that these retirements were made on the recommendation of the department, and, that the Civil Service Commission had concurred in those recommendations. I have never heard of anyone concurring in anything until an opinion has been indicated. Apparently the Civil Service Commission had nothing to do with this matter in the first place, and I want to know who made the recommendations and for what reason.

In this case, the reason for the reduction was the transfer to the western provinces. The head of the branch certainly was the man who would best know who could most efficiently carry on the services which the Dominion was to perform. The personnel would be determined and the recommendations would be made by the head of that branch. The Civil Service Commission were advised immediately; their officials were working with us in the department; they knew from day to day, if not practically from hour to hour, what was being done, and I use the word "concur" in that sense.

I am not taking this particular branch as a sample, but I am taking the department when these retirements were being made. Does the minister mean that officials of the Civil Service Commission worked in conjunction with officials of the department, sat together and decided who was to go, or does he mean to say, as his answer would imply, that these recommendations were made by officials of the department and then submitted to the Civil Service Commission which later, as the minister said, concurred in them?
I do not think I can make the matter any plainer to the committee than I have already done; I detailed the steps that were taken and the manner in which it was done.

Item agreed to.
Amount required to meet expenses of lake of the Woods control board, $8,000.
How does the 82,000 reduction come about?

This reduction is simply carrying on the work in a more economical manner. I can give the various items if the hon. member would like to have them. They are as follows:
One senior engineering clerk, $2,160.
One hydrometric recorder, $1,800.
One junior hydrometric recorder, $1,140.
Gauge readers, $700.
Field expenses, $1,700.
Travelling and incidental expenses, $500.
I am sorry I cannot give the comparative figures for the last fiscal year, but it might be that the reduction is explained by a lesser amount for field expenses and for travelling and incidental expenses.

Item agreed to.
To provide for the expenses connected with the national parks of Canada, historic sites, care of indigents in the parks, the appointment of stipendiary magistrates in the parks and the payment of their remuneration, etc., $1,319,200.

I should like to put in a special plea on behalf of the national park at Prince Albert. As my hon. friend knows, the Prince Albert national park is, with one exception, the latest of the parks to be developed. Not merely is it helping to meet the recreation needs of the more immediate localities, but it has come to be recognized as of service to the entire province of Saskatchewan. An association known as the Saskatchewan Provincial National Park Association has been formed which I believe includes representatives from all the constituencies in the province, so that what I am about to say will be said on behalf of the province as a whole and not merely in the interests of the constituency which I have the honour to represent in the House of Commons.
What I wish to direct the minister's attention particularly bo is the fact that the park being in the preliminary stage of development, a great deal of work has to be carried on there which years ago was completed in the older parks, especially such work as is required for sanitary improvement purposes and the subdivision of lots so that citizens of the province who are anxious to acquire small properties in the park may avail themselves of the opportunity to build immediately. While I notice the minister is cutting down the appropriation for national parks, I hope the last cut will be made before it comes to Prince Albert. I trust that for this particular year, for the reasons I have mentioned, that not only will he find it unnecessary to cut down at all as respects Prince Albert National Park, but rather that he will in-

Supply-Interior-National Parks
crease a little the outlay there. An increase is necessary in order to enable these preliminary developments to be made. The thousands of people who visited the park last year and the year before were very much embarrassed by the fact that the arrangements generally were not at all adequate to the needs of such numbers of people visiting the park and not at all such as to permit of persons residing there for any length of time. The situation as regards sanitary requirements, and accommodations generally has already become quite serious. The minister is probably aware of it as representations I know have been made from other quarters as well. I wish, however, to stress the importance of the much needed development along lines of sanitation and particularly as regards the subdivision of lots so that building may be carried on at once. Especially in weather such as this, my hon. friend will be able to appreciate what the one stretch of country in northern Saskatchewan which has been set apart as a National park, the one part that has Lakes, rivers and forests in abundance, must mean to the rest of the province as a whole when it is remembered that the rest of the province, as my hon. friend well knows, for the most part does not enjoy anything of the kind. I am sure I hardly need mention the matter to the minister; I know he has had it under consideration, but I know I speak for all members from Saskatchewan, regardless of which side of the house they are on, when I make this special plea on behalf of the Prince Albert park.

I am sorry to note the decrease in the amount to be spent on the national parks. At this time when we have such a large amount of unemployment, we might very well undertake in the parks work which under ordinary circumstances might not be undertaken for a good many years to come. At the present time we are paying out large sums of money for direct relief purposes and there is nothing to show at the end of the season for these large amounts spent on direct relief. It would be far better for these men who are necessarily in receipt of relief, to do something in return. I do n.ot mean to say that they should simply have their board or anything of that kind. They should receive proper pay for doing good work. But I believe this would be a splendid opportunity to organize on a large scale relief works. Perhaps even the Minister of the Interior might take this matter into consideration. I know there is a tendency to throw the whole burden upon the IMr. Mackenzie King.]
Department of Labour and to say they must work out a scheme, but it ought to be worked out in connection with the different departments. The Minister of the Interior would be very well advised largely to extend the expenditures in his department at this particular time.
In connection with national parks, what progress is being made in the province of New Brunswick? The question of a national park in New Brunswick has been discussed in the last two years-

Please let us
first get an answer about Prince Albert.
The minister bowed to you.
I want something more than a bow, something that can go on Hansard.

I am sorry if I appeared
discourteous to the right hon. gentleman, but other members rose as I was about to speak. I can say with the right hon. leader of the opposition that the people of Canada, I believe, are increasingly coming to a realization and a proper appreciation of what these areas which have been set aside as national parks mean to the country, and not only from a dollars and cents standpoint, which is considerable. and which can be augmented It may not be out of place for me to say that I believe our national parks can be made a wonderful financial asset to the Dominion for they approach the ideal where you can both eat your cake and have it. That is, our scenery does not disappear with use. It is only necessary for those who administer these parks to see that their natural beauty is preserved and that the attractions and relaxation that they afford not only to our own people but to people of other countries are maintained. I appreciate to the fullest extent the concern which the right hon. leader of the opposition feels for the Prince Albert park. It is one of the latest parks to be established, the only later one being that established in the Riding mountains in my own province of Manitoba. I deeply regret any curtailment of the work which might otherwise be carried on in these parks for I believe that the people of the country-I am speaking generally now of those inhabiting the cities and the countryside-increasingly appreciate the benefits which may accrue to them and their families from a sojourn in these areas.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF CHEQUES WITH NO FUNDS OR INSUFFICIENT FUNDS IN BANK

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, June 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Neill for the second reading of Bill No. 43 to amend the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ISSUANCE OF CHEQUES WITH NO FUNDS OR INSUFFICIENT FUNDS IN BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read over this
bill and have heard the discussion which so far has taken place upon it, and speaking for myself I do not think the bill as drawn will advance the objects which the hon. member who proposes the measure has in view. The bill has also been examined by the officers of the Justice department, and while I do not want to prejudice the bill in the opinion of the house, I may say that the bill is not favourably viewed by them, or by other parties who have communicated with the Justice department on the subject. Personally I want to admit that I have received a good many letters from retail merchants throughout the country favouring the passage of this bill. I also have received a considerable number of protests, among others one from the Canadian Bankers' Association, and several from boards of trade and chambers of commerce and bodies of that kind.
The object which the hon. member seeks to attain by this bill is a very laudable' one. It is to decrease, if possible, the habit of issuing cheques for cash or in payment for goods for which there is not in the bank at the time a' sufficient balance to the credit of the drawer of the cheque; consequently the cheque
is dishonoured at the bank and returned to the drawee. We have a section now in the criminal code, as everyone knows, to provide against obtaining money or goods by false pretences. Many prosecutions have taken place under that section in respect of dishonoured cheques, but it generally has been considered by magistrates that when a man has some balance in the bank and issues a cheque, he has not done so fraudulently or with intent to defraud, because it can always be said he assumed he had credit at the bank and was not aware of the exact balance which stood to his credit at the time he issued the cheque. In that way many issuers of what we call worthless cheques have been relieved of responsibility under that section of the code which provides against obtaining money by false pretences.
The view I take is that the proposed amendment would open the door to the issuers of worthless cheques-would invite them to continue the practice rather than discourage them. It actually lays down that if a man issues a cheque when he has no bank account, or thinking he has a sufficient balance at the bank, or thinking that the bank will honour the cheque, he is not guilty of an offence. Under the law to-day if a man issues a cheque honestly thinking that he has a sufficient balance in the bank to meet it, or thinking that his credit is good enough at the bank to ensure that the cheque will be paid, it cannot be said that he does so fraudulently. But if he issues a cheque upon a bank where he has no account and no banking credit, he would be guilty of fraud. This bill merely points out a comparatively safe way to the issuer of these cheques to go ahead. As long as the issuer can establish that he thought he had some small balance in the bank, or that he thought he had credit at the bank, he will not be liable in respect of his worthless cheque if he makes the default good within a reasonable time.
I cannot see, Mr. Speaker, how this proposal will secure people who receive such cheques in payment for money or goods or in settlement of accounts to any greater extent than they are secured at the present time. If my hon. friend would propose an amendment making it an offence to issue a cheque for which there are no funds or not sufficient funds in the bank, he would go a long way towards stopping the issuance of worthless cheques, but he has not done so. In his amendment he merely says that any man who issues a cheque and has reasonable grounds to believe that he has some balance at the bank or that the bank will honour his cheque is not
Criminal Code

liable to prosecution. I think you would very effectively stop this pernicious practice of issuing bad cheques if you were to provide by an amendment that a man who issues such a cheque, without funds or without sufficient funds at the bank, is liable to prosecution and conviction. In its present form I fear that the bill will merely invite issuers of bad cheques to proceed as they have been doing in the past, and will render the operation a little less hazardous.

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF CHEQUES WITH NO FUNDS OR INSUFFICIENT FUNDS IN BANK
speechtext: I have had a great many communications from business men of the city of Vancouver, endorsing this amendment. After carefully reading the bill I thought it was so framed that at least it would not work a hardship upon anyone; I thought the words "within a reasonable time" would take care of any contingency of that kind, and I was prepared to support the amendment. But after listening to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), and admitting that he knows much more about these matters than I do, if he believes this would rather open the way for that which we are trying to prevent, then I have nothing further to say. If the mover can so amend his bill as to accomplish what we have in mind, I shall be pleased to support it.

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF CHEQUES WITH NO FUNDS OR INSUFFICIENT FUNDS IN BANK
speechtext:
I
find myself very much in the position of my hon. friend, from Vancouver South (Mr. Mac-Innis). I also have received several hundred communications supporting the principle of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), and I may admit quite frankly that I have not received a single representation in opposition to it.
With all due respect to the very considered opinion of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), I do not think he described in exact detail the purport of section 1 of the bill, the purpose of which is to amend section 405 of the criminal code, which deals with obtaining goods by false pretences. With the permission of the house I should like to read exactly the words of the amendment:
Everyone who draws and issues a cheque on a chartered bank in Canada for the payment of money and at the time he draws and issues the cheque has no funds or insufficient funds on deposit in that bank to meet the cheque, and has no reasonable grounds to believe that the

cheque will be paid by the bank, and to whom no credit has been extended by the bank at the time of the presentation of the cheque . . . .
If the section stopped there I believe most of the representations submitted by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice would be justified, but the sponsor of the bill goes further and says:
.... and who, upon the refusal of the bank to honour the cheque does not, within a reasonable time, deposit in the bank to his credit a sufficient amount to meet the cheque ....
In other words, according to my interpretation of this section, there is a double opportunity offered here. The innocent, bona fide issuer of a cheque without sufficient funds in the bank to his credit has a second opportunity after the refusal of the bank to honour the cheque. The section proceeds:
.... does not, within a reasonable time, deposit in the bank to his credit a sufficient amount to meet the cheque or pay the amount of such cheque to the holder thereof ....
If he does not do this he is guilty of an offence. I consider that while the section may not be perfect it provides a very reasonable protection both to the issuer of a cheque in good faith and to our retail merchants. All the representations I have received have come from the city of Vancouver, not only from retail merchants 'but from many organizations, all of which are members of the Vancouver board of trade. My hon. friend told the house that he had received representations against the principle of this bill from boards of trade and banks, and of course I accept his word. I am quite prepared to believe that representations against this section might come from banks, but I do believe that at least the principle the hon. member for Comox-Alberni seeks to establish would meet with the approval and sanction of ninety per cent of the business organizations throughout Canada, and would be approved also by ninety-five per cent of those who issue cheques in the ordinary course of business.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) should be congratulated upon bringing in this amendment, but when one reads it carefully it will be seen that it would be rather hard for a magistrate to apply the law. Who can say that a person had no reasonable grounds to believe that the cheque would be paid by the bank? A distinction should be made here between a man who has an account at the bank and one who has not.

Criminal Code
The man having no account at the bank should be found guilty, while the man who has an account should be considered in a different way.
Consider the case of a man who has a current account with the bank, and who has endorsed a note signed by a third party, which note has been credited to his account. He sends a renewal of that note to the other person, telling him to take it to the bank, but the other person neglects to do so. As a consequence this man finds himself overdrawn. Thinking he is not overdrawn he issues a cheque on his account which is returned marked n.s.f., because the note has been charged to his account without his knowledge. Would it be fair to find that man guilty? I think not.

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF CHEQUES WITH NO FUNDS OR INSUFFICIENT FUNDS IN BANK
speechtext:
He has
a reasonable time in which to make it good.

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF CHEQUES WITH NO FUNDS OR INSUFFICIENT FUNDS IN BANK
speechtext:
Supposing this man has a certain amount of money coming to him monthly, say S100, S200 or S300, and that money is deposited in the bank. He has a note for $500 signed by a third .person, and through the negligence of that third person in not returning the renewal in time he finds himself overdrawn. He cannot put in the bank more money than he receives monthly. That is one difficulty. Then it would be pretty hard for the magistrate to define the words "has no reasonable grounds to believe." This man would have reasonable grounds to believe that the cheque would be honoured, but because of the neglect of the other person there are not sufficient funds in his account to meet that cheque when it is presented to the bank.
Then there is another point. The section contains the words:
.... and who, upon the refusal of the bank to honour the cheque does not, within a reasonable time, deposit in the bank to his credit a sufficient amount to meet the cheque. . . .
What is "reasonable time"? Is it three days of grace, a week, or a month? We are not told. "Reasonable time" is not defined, and it should be defined; otherwise magistrates are likely to hold different views until the question is settled by the supreme court. And very seldom do these offences come before the Supreme Court of Canada. My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni modifies his amendment by making it a criminal offence for anyone who has no account with a bank to issue a cheque, leaving aside the man who has an account when he issues a cheque or who believes that the bank will honour his cheque for special reasons. This, I think, is the only distinction that can be made between those who issue cheques in good faith, though they may not have sufficient funds to meet them, and those who issue cheques simply as a means of obtaining goods, which they virtually steal. If my hon friend will make that amendment clear, I shall gladly support it. But if the proposed change is left as it stands, I cannot reasonably accept it, although in principle I agree with the hon. member.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE (Montmagny): If the theory of the hon. member for Temis-couata is accepted, there is no need of this bill because to-day the moment a man issues a cheque without an account he is found guilty of false pretences. There is, therefore, no need of such an amendment as is proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I am inclined to agree with the Minister of Justice. This bill will afford a defence in cases which are doubtful. When a man issues a cheque without an account or for which he has not sufficient funds in the bank, the magistrate can only decide that he is guilty of false pretences. This bill would furnish a defence that could not be quashed, because it asks the magistrate to be the judge of the intent of the accused. The accused might have thought when he issued the cheque that he had funds, or he might have had reason to believe that the bank would honour the cheque. This would establish his bona fides and the charge would fail. But this bill goes further. It tells people that they may run the risk of committing a felony, of issuing a cheque without sufficient funds, and if they are caught they will have a chance of defending themselves by depositing the money in the bank. This is an unsound principle, which can have but one effect: people will be only too ready to issue cheques when they have no funds. It defeats its own purpose, and I think the house should vote against it.

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF CHEQUES WITH NO FUNDS OR INSUFFICIENT FUNDS IN BANK
speechtext: I am wholly in accord with the principle of the bill, but I think it might be differently worded to meet the purpose it has in view. For that reason I shall be glad to vote for the second reading and let it go to committee.

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF CHEQUES WITH NO FUNDS OR INSUFFICIENT FUNDS IN BANK
speechtext:
This
bill will be strongly favoured by a large body of creditors because it is the best method yet devised of using the criminal code for collecting debts. I think I know the reason why the bill was introduced. It is an offence under the criminal code to obtain goods or money by false pretences. If you issue a cheque when you have no account and obtain
Criminal Code

goods or money thereby, you are obtaining such goods or money by false pretences. If you issue a cheque on an account in which you have some funds but not sufficient, you may be obtaining goods by false pretences, because in your own mind you may know that there are not sufficient funds. And many people follow that practice rather than go without an account. The purpose of the bill was to get at those who issue cheques in return for goods or money when they know they have not sufficient funds, thus obtaining the goods by false pretences. It is difficult to prove the element of false intent in such an event, because there is money in the bank. In this country there is unfortunately a large debtor class, and it is a common practice for the collector to bring pressure to bear upon people when they are not able to pay for goods they have already got. They will say to them, "Can't you pay to-day? If not, can you make monthly payments?" The debtor may be able to do that, and the collector says, "Give us a series of post-dated cheques to cover the debt by monthly payments". The person who has taken the cheque gives nothing in return beyond an extension of time for payment of a debt which otherwise would not be collected. What will happen next? As soon as one of these cheques is overdue the collector goes up to the debtor and says, "There are not sufficient funds to meet your cheque. I want that money within a reasonable time or I will put the criminal law in force against you". If the bill could provide for the man who obtains goods or money on the strength of an n.s.f. cheque, I should be more inclined to support it. But it goes further and provides that where a man gives an n.s.f. cheque in payment of an old outstanding debt he shall be regarded as a criminal and shall go to jail because of his inability to make good the cheque. I am strongly opposed to that feature of the bill and must vote against it.

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF CHEQUES WITH NO FUNDS OR INSUFFICIENT FUNDS IN BANK
speechtext:
Under the
law as it stands, it is difficult to secure a conviction. I agree entirely with the opinion expressed by the Minister of Justice. I believe that if this amendment becomes law it will open the door wider to the practice of fraud and deception in the issuing of n.s.f. cheques. If a man were charged under this bill, what is the first question counsel would ask? He would ask how many ingredients constitute the offence. How many elements would have to be proved before the accused was found guilty? Reading the section carefully, one will see that for a man to be found guilty under this provision the crown, upon 
whom the burden of proof always rests, would have to prove four distinct ingredients before the offence could be fully established. For instance, the crown would have to prove that the accused had no funds or insufficient funds on deposit in a bank to meet the cheque. It would have to prove that the accused had no reasonable ground to believe that the cheque would be paid by the bank. It would have to prove that the accused was a person to whom no credit had been extended by the bank at the time of the presentation of the cheque. And it would have to prove that the accused had not within a reasonable time deposited sufficient funds to meet the cheque. There would also be a doubt as to the meaning of "a reasonable time". The clause which reads, "and has no reasonable grounds to believe that the cheque will be paid by the bank" is an element in the offence which could not be circumvented by the crown.
I know that many representations have been made by commercial organizations to have the law amended in this respect. A prominent commercial institution in the city of Winnipeg proposed that I draft an amendment to this particular section of the code in the hope that the measure would be passed by parliament. I do not think the institutions which are supporting this proposal realize that the door is being opened to a wider extent. If this bill becomes law it would be almost impossible to convict a man for issuing an n.s.f. cheque. In many cases our criminal courts are being turned into collection agencies. If the money is paid the person who lays the information will very often go before the magistrate and ask that it be withdrawn. The practice in Winnipeg has been not to turn the criminal courts into collection agencies, and I do not believe that a court of criminal law should be used in this way. Our courts would be glutted with all sorts of informations and they could not carry on their work as well as they do at the present time.
The introducer of this bill (Mr. Neill) should be congratulated upon the attempt he has made to improve the law, but I believe the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie.) was right when he said that if this proposed legislation becomes law the door would be opened much wider to facilitate the efforts of those who are obtaining money and goods under false pretences. This is a difficult point in criminal law, and I do not think we ought to legislate upon it in haste. For these reasons I intend to oppose the bill.
